newsitem.title: USA: Engineer's colorblindness cited in N.J. train wreck.
newsitem.headline: Engineer's colorblindness cited in N.J. train wreck.

text.p: The engineer of a commuter train that ran a stop signal and collided head-on with another train last year had an an eye condition that kept him from perceiving the light was red, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.
Three people died including the engineers of both trains and 158 passengers were injured.

The National Transportation Safety Board said the engineer of the eastbound New Jersey Transit train had failed to report his diabetic eye condition and resulting colourblindness during medical examinations.

This was the likely cause of the Feb. 9, 1996, collision of his train with a westbound one near Secaucus, it said. It said contributing to the accident was a doctor's use of an eye examination not intended to measure colour blindness.

The board said the engineer's acquired red-green colour deficiency caused him to interpret the stop signal to be either a "restricting" signal or a "medium approach" signal, either of which would have allowed him to proceed.

It said the doctor's faulty test procedure resulted in the engineer being wrongly certified and recommended that the Federal Railroad Administration revise its current colour vision testing requirement for engineers to specify the test to be used, testing procedures and qualifying standards.
It also recommended that no person with a known medical deficiency that would make him unable to be certified be allowed to act as an engineer.

The board also told New Jersey Transit to improve its train emergency evacuation procedures and said the agency, the Association of American Railroads, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and the United Transportation Union should widely publicise the facts of the accident.
